subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Ralph Nader Shakes the Industry
description: Learn Ralph Nader Shakes the Industry in one minute.

hook.text: In 1965, a young lawyer published a book that terrified the entire auto industry.

buildup.text: Ralph Nader's Unsafe at Any Speed exposed the Corvair's dangerous rear suspension design.

discovery.text: The book revealed that car companies knew about deadly flaws but chose profits over safety.

twist.text: GM hired detectives to follow Nader and dig up dirt—when exposed, the scandal backfired.

climax.text: Congress passed the Motor Vehicle Safety Act in 1966, forcing national safety standards.

punchline.text: One book rewrote the rules of car safety forever.

quiz.question: What did Ralph Nader's book Unsafe at Any Speed expose?

details.summary: Ralph Nader's 1965 book Unsafe at Any Speed exposed how automakers prioritized style over safety, sparking public outrage that led directly to federal vehicle safety regulations in the United States.
details.whyItMatters: Nader's crusade forced the creation of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration and mandatory safety standards, fundamentally changing how the auto industry approaches occupant protection.
takeaways: Nader exposed design flaws in the Chevrolet Corvair
Public pressure led to the 1966 National Traffic Safety Act
NHTSA was created to enforce vehicle safety standards

faq.question: Was the Chevrolet Corvair actually as dangerous as Nader claimed?
faq.answer: Later studies found the Corvair's handling was comparable to other cars of its era. However, Nader's broader point about industry-wide neglect of safety engineering was well documented and valid.

faq.question: What regulations came directly from Nader's advocacy?
faq.answer: The 1966 National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act mandated seatbelts, padded dashboards, and energy-absorbing steering columns in all new cars. It was the first comprehensive federal auto safety law.
